paragraphs.text: Osteogenesis imperfecta type XIII is an autosomal recessive bone fragility disorder with recurrent fractures. Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) described sibs with severe progressive bone deformity, short stature and large umbilical hernias, classified as OI type III. Other patients have bone mineral density that is normal or increased rather than reduced (Asharani et al., 2012; Valencia et al., 2014). Fahiminiya et al. (2015) described fractures mainly of the lower limbs with a bone mineralization defect.

paragraphs.text: Munns et al. (2004) described 3 unrelated children with an apparently novel bone fragility disorder associated with an idiopathic mineralization defect. Recurrent lower limb fractures began when the children started bearing weight. The patients had none of the phenotypic, radiologic or histomorphometric features of known bone fragility disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta, idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis or mild autosomal dominant osteopetrosis. Radiographs showed increased metaphyseal trabeculation, normal to increased cortical thickness, and no evidence of rickets or osteomalacia. Areal and volumetric bone mineral density of the lumbar spine showed no major alteration. In 1 patient, peripheral quantitative computed tomography of the radius showed increased cortical thickness and increased total and trabecular volumetric bone mineral density. Iliac bone biopsies showed little of the birefringent pattern of normal lamellar bone. Histomorphometry showed osteomalacia, with a prolonged mineralization lag time and a decreased mineral apposition rate. There was no biochemical evidence of abnormal calcium or phosphate metabolism, and type I collagen mutation analysis was negative. Munns et al. (2004) concluded that this was a bone fragility disorder of moderate severity, with fractures mainly of the lower limbs and accumulation of osteoid due to an intrinsic mineralization defect.

paragraphs.text: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) studied 2 sibs with severe autosomal recessive OI born to Egyptian parents who were first cousins. The proband, a 15-year-old girl, had a left tibial fracture noted after a normal full-term vaginal delivery. Thereafter she had frequent spontaneous fractures of the upper and lower limbs, averaging 10 to 15 per year. She had a triangular face, broad forehead, wide palpebral fissures, long eyelashes, faint blue sclerae, long philtrum, thin lips and prominent ears. Gross motor development was delayed, and she could not stand unsupported. Mental development was normal, and she had no dentinogenesis imperfecta. Her thorax was relatively large and compressed the abdomen. She had a large umbilical hernia (5 cm wide and 7 cm long) containing abdominal contents. Other findings were generalized hypotonia, muscle wasting, nocturnal enuresis and generalized hirsutism. Her skin had normal stretchability, with no bruising or scars. She had severe generalized bone deformities with pain on touch, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible elbows, wrists and interphalangeal joints, limited knee movement, kyphoscoliosis and pectus carinatum. Radiographs showed deformed long bones with multiple fractures and callus formation and lack of bone modeling. The distal femoral metaphyses were wide, and the tibiae and fibulae were thin and serpentine. Radiographs also showed S-curve thoracolumbar scoliosis with platyspondyly, generalized decreased bone density, and wormian bones. At 13 years of age, her weight was -3.8 SD, length -11.5 SD and head circumference -3.0 SD. At 15 years, DEXA showed borderline osteoporosis (Z-scores -2.22 at the hip and -2.13 at the spine).

paragraphs.text: The proband's 5-year-old brother had bilateral femoral bowing on fetal ultrasound, and both femora were fractured at birth (Martínez-Glez et al., 2012). He had recurrent fractures at an average rate of 15 per year. His facial features resembled his sister's, and he had normal mentality and no dentinogenesis imperfecta. He could not stand unsupported. He had generalized bone deformities, hyperextensible joints, arachnodactyly, and a large umbilical hernia (4 cm wide and 5 cm long). Radiographs showed wormian bones, deformed long bones lacking modeling, fractures with callus formation, scoliosis, platyspondyly and a wide symphysis pubis. His weight was -3.7 SD and length -7.2 SD, with normal head circumference. DEXA showed borderline osteoporosis at the spine (Z-score -1.63) and osteoporosis at the left femur (Z-score -2.75). In both sibs, audiologic and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable, serum calcium and phosphate were normal, and alkaline phosphatase was slightly high. Both were diagnosed with OI type III according to the Sillence classification (Sillence et al., 1979).

paragraphs.text: In 2 Egyptian sibs with severe autosomal recessive OI born to first-cousin parents, Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) found a homozygous c.747C-G transversion in exon 6 of the BMP1 gene, predicting a phe249-to-leu (F249L) substitution. The variant was identified by sequencing BMP1, a candidate gene within a region of homozygosity on chromosome 8p. Phe249 lies in the protease domain and is conserved in all members of the astacin family of metalloproteases. The parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous. The variant was absent from 100 control chromosomes of the same ethnic origin and 884 European control chromosomes, and COL1A1 and COL1A2 sequencing in 1 patient found no mutations. Patient fibroblasts showed reduced C-terminal processing of type I procollagen, with less pN-alpha-1(I) relative to pC-alpha-1(I) and less free C-terminal propeptide. Fibroblasts from a heterozygous sib showed slight impairment. In NIH3T3 cells and human primary fibroblasts, overexpression of wildtype mTLD (the longer BMP1 isoform) enhanced C-terminal processing of pro-alpha-1(I), whereas the mutant protein did not. Mutant protein levels in patient cells were not significantly reduced.
